course.title: Linear Algebra
course.level: first university course in linear algebra; assumes comfort with vectors and high-school algebra (18.02 is MIT's formal prerequisite, but calculus is not required)
course.textbook: Gilbert Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra, 4th or 5th edition
parts: Unit I: Ax = b and the Four Subspaces
Unit II: Least Squares, Determinants and Eigenvalues
Unit III: Positive Definite Matrices and Applications
course.unit_order_source: OCW course navigation (sources/019-resource-index.txt lists the same sequence)

units.title: The Geometry of Linear Equations
units.part: Unit I: Ax = b and the Four Subspaces
units.summary: Three ways to read n equations in n unknowns: the row picture (lines or planes meeting at a point), the column picture (a combination of A's columns that reaches b) and the matrix form Ax = b. Strang's 2x - y = 0, -x + 2y = 3 is solved by (1, 2) in both pictures, and the lecture asks when the columns can reach every b.
key_ideas: singular case: columns in a plane

units.title: An Overview of Key Ideas
units.part: Unit I: Ax = b and the Four Subspaces
units.summary: A bird's-eye tour (borrowed from Strang's 18.085) of the path vectors -> matrices -> subspaces: Ax is a combination of columns, the difference matrix A has a sum matrix as its inverse, and the cyclic difference matrix C has dependent columns, so Cx = b is solvable only when b1 + b2 + b3 = 0 (its column space is a plane).

units.title: Elimination with Matrices
units.part: Unit I: Ax = b and the Four Subspaces
units.summary: Gaussian elimination subtracts multiples of pivot rows to reach an upper-triangular U, then back-substitutes. Each step is an elimination matrix E_ij multiplying from the left, row exchanges are permutation matrices, and elimination fails only when a zero pivot cannot be repaired by a row exchange.

units.title: Multiplication and Inverse Matrices
units.part: Unit I: Ax = b and the Four Subspaces
units.summary: Five views of AB = C: entry as row times column, columns of C as combinations of A's columns, rows of C as combinations of B's rows, a sum of column-times-row pieces, and block multiplication. A square A is invertible exactly when no nonzero x solves Ax = 0, and Gauss-Jordan elimination turns [A I] into [I A^-1].
key_ideas: column and row pictures of AB

units.title: Factorization into A = LU
units.part: Unit I: Ax = b and the Four Subspaces
units.summary: Elimination recorded as a factorization: the multipliers drop straight into a lower-triangular L with A = LU (or A = LDU with the pivots in D). Along the way (AB)^-1 = B^-1 A^-1, (AB)^T = B^T A^T, elimination costs about n^3/3 operations, and row exchanges lead to PA = LU.
key_ideas: inverse and transpose of a product

units.title: Transposes, Permutations, Vector Spaces
units.part: Unit I: Ax = b and the Four Subspaces
units.summary: Permutation matrices (n! of them, with P^-1 = P^T) complete PA = LU; transposes give symmetric matrices, and R^T R is always symmetric. Then the leap to vector spaces and subspaces: sets closed under addition and scalar multiplication, such as lines and planes through the origin in R3, with the column space of A as the first example.

units.title: Column Space and Nullspace
units.part: Unit I: Ax = b and the Four Subspaces
units.summary: The column space C(A) is all combinations of the columns, so Ax = b is solvable exactly when b lies in C(A). The nullspace N(A) is all solutions of Ax = 0 and is a subspace of R^n, while the solutions of Ax = b with b != 0 do not form a subspace; intersections of subspaces are subspaces, unions usually are not.

units.title: Solving Ax = 0: Pivot Variables, Special Solutions
units.part: Unit I: Ax = b and the Four Subspaces
units.summary: Elimination on any rectangular matrix gives an echelon form U and then the reduced row echelon form R. The r pivot columns and n - r free columns organise the nullspace: setting one free variable to 1 and the rest to 0 gives a special solution, and the special solutions (the columns of N = [-F; I]) form a basis of N(A).
key_ideas: reduced row echelon form R = [I F; 0 0]

units.title: Solving Ax = b: Row Reduced Form R
units.part: Unit I: Ax = b and the Four Subspaces
units.summary: Ax = b is solvable when b satisfies the same combinations that zero out rows of A; the complete solution is one particular solution (free variables set to 0) plus every nullspace vector. The rank decides the cases: r = m = n gives exactly one solution, r = n < m gives 0 or 1, r = m < n gives infinitely many, r < m and r < n gives 0 or infinitely many.

units.title: Independence, Basis and Dimension
units.part: Unit I: Ax = b and the Four Subspaces
units.summary: Vectors are independent when no nontrivial combination gives zero, i.e. the matrix with those columns has N(A) = {0}; more than n vectors in R^n are always dependent. A basis is an independent spanning set, every basis of a space has the same size (its dimension), and so dim C(A) = r and dim N(A) = n - r.

units.title: The Four Fundamental Subspaces
units.part: Unit I: Ax = b and the Four Subspaces
units.summary: Every m by n matrix has four subspaces: the column space C(A) and left nullspace N(A^T) in R^m, the row space C(A^T) and nullspace N(A) in R^n, with dimensions r, m - r, r and n - r. Elimination EA = R produces bases for all four, and the space of 3 by 3 matrices previews vector spaces whose vectors are matrices.
key_ideas: dimensions r, n - r, r, m - r

units.title: Matrix Spaces; Rank 1; Small World Graphs
units.part: Unit I: Ax = b and the Four Subspaces
units.summary: Vector spaces beyond R^n: the 9-dimensional space of 3 by 3 matrices with its symmetric (dimension 6), upper-triangular (6) and diagonal (3) subspaces, and the solutions of y'' + y = 0 with basis cos x, sin x. Every rank-one matrix is a column times a row, u v^T, and small-world graphs open the study of networks.

units.title: Graphs, Networks, Incidence Matrices
units.part: Unit I: Ax = b and the Four Subspaces
units.summary: The incidence matrix of a directed graph (one row per edge with -1 and +1) turns circuit laws into linear algebra: its nullspace holds constant potentials, independent loops span the left nullspace (Kirchhoff's current law A^T y = 0), and dim N(A^T) = m - r gives Euler's formula nodes - edges + loops = 1.

units.title: Exam 1 Review
units.part: Unit I: Ax = b and the Four Subspaces
units.summary: Review of Unit I through sample questions: the possible dimensions of a span, rank and reduced echelon form of stacked block matrices such as [R; 2R], reconstructing A from the complete solution of Ax = b, and short true/false checks on subspaces, rank and invertibility, plus a recitation on exam-style problem solving.
key_ideas: recovering A from a complete solution

units.title: Exam 1
units.part: Unit I: Ax = b and the Four Subspaces
units.summary: The Unit I exam: deduce m, n and the rank from which right-hand sides are solvable, invert A from a sequence of elimination matrices E21, E31, E23 and recover A and L, find bases for the column space and nullspace of a 3 by 4 matrix depending on c, and read off what R = rref(A) says about A's columns.

units.title: Orthogonal Vectors and Subspaces
units.part: Unit II: Least Squares, Determinants and Eigenvalues
units.summary: Vectors are orthogonal when x^T y = 0 (equivalently |x|^2 + |y|^2 = |x + y|^2). The row space is the orthogonal complement of the nullspace in R^n, and the column space of the left nullspace in R^m. Because N(A^T A) = N(A), the matrix A^T A is invertible exactly when A has independent columns, the doorway to least squares.

units.title: Projections onto Subspaces
units.part: Unit II: Least Squares, Determinants and Eigenvalues
units.summary: Projecting b onto the line through a gives p = a (a^T b / a^T a) and the rank-one projection matrix P = a a^T / a^T a. Projecting onto the column space of A requires the error e = b - A x_hat to be perpendicular to every column, giving A^T A x_hat = A^T b and P = A (A^T A)^-1 A^T with P^2 = P and P^T = P.
key_ideas: normal equations A^T A x_hat = A^T b

units.title: Projection Matrices and Least Squares
units.part: Unit II: Least Squares, Determinants and Eigenvalues
units.summary: Least squares fits a line C + Dt to points no line passes through by projecting b onto the column space: solve A^T A x_hat = A^T b, and the errors e = b - p lie in the left nullspace, perpendicular to the columns. The lecture fits (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 2) with the best line 2/3 + t/2.
key_ideas: A^T A invertible for independent columns

units.title: Orthogonal Matrices and Gram-Schmidt
units.part: Unit II: Least Squares, Determinants and Eigenvalues
units.summary: Orthonormal columns give a matrix Q with Q^T Q = I (and Q^-1 = Q^T when Q is square), so projection becomes P = Q Q^T and least squares becomes x_hat = Q^T b. Gram-Schmidt turns independent vectors into orthonormal ones by subtracting their projections onto earlier directions, which factors A = QR with R upper triangular.

units.title: Properties of Determinants
units.part: Unit II: Least Squares, Determinants and Eigenvalues
units.summary: The determinant is pinned down by three properties: det I = 1, a row exchange reverses the sign, and det is linear in each row separately. From these follow the rest: equal rows give 0, row operations leave det unchanged, a triangular det is the product of the pivots, det A = 0 exactly when A is singular, det AB = det A det B and det A^T = det A.
key_ideas: det AB = det A det B

units.title: Determinant Formulas and Cofactors
units.part: Unit II: Least Squares, Determinants and Eigenvalues
units.summary: Splitting each row by linearity gives the big formula, a sum of n! signed products with one entry from each row and column. Grouping terms by the first row gives the cofactor expansion det A = a11 C11 + ... + a1n C1n, applied to tridiagonal matrices of 1's whose determinants repeat with period 6.

units.title: Cramer's Rule, Inverse Matrix and Volume
units.part: Unit II: Least Squares, Determinants and Eigenvalues
units.summary: Cofactors give an explicit inverse A^-1 = C^T / det A, which yields Cramer's rule x_j = det B_j / det A (B_j is A with column j replaced by b). The absolute value of det A is the volume of the box whose edges are the rows, which gives areas of parallelograms and triangles straight from coordinates.
key_ideas: area of a triangle from coordinates

units.title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
units.part: Unit II: Least Squares, Determinants and Eigenvalues
units.summary: An eigenvector keeps its direction under A: Ax = lambda x. Eigenvalues solve det(A - lambda I) = 0, their sum is the trace and their product the determinant. Examples include projections (lambda = 0 and 1), rotations with complex eigenvalues, and triangular matrices with a repeated eigenvalue but too few eigenvectors.

units.title: Diagonalization and Powers of A
units.part: Unit II: Least Squares, Determinants and Eigenvalues
units.summary: With n independent eigenvectors in S, A = S Lambda S^-1 and A^k = S Lambda^k S^-1, so u_(k+1) = A u_k is solved by u_k = c1 lambda1^k x1 + ... + cn lambdan^k xn. Distinct eigenvalues guarantee independent eigenvectors, and the Fibonacci numbers grow like ((1 + sqrt 5)/2)^k.

units.title: Differential Equations and exp(At)
units.part: Unit II: Least Squares, Determinants and Eigenvalues
units.summary: Systems du/dt = Au are solved by pure exponentials e^(lambda t) x, so u(t) = c1 e^(lambda1 t) x1 + c2 e^(lambda2 t) x2. Stability needs Re(lambda) < 0 and a steady state needs lambda = 0; the matrix exponential e^(At) = S e^(Lambda t) S^-1 comes from the power series, and y'' + b y' + k y = 0 becomes a 2 by 2 first-order system.

units.title: Markov Matrices; Fourier Series
units.part: Unit II: Least Squares, Determinants and Eigenvalues
units.summary: Markov matrices (nonnegative entries, columns summing to 1) always have lambda = 1 with all other |lambda| <= 1, so A^k u0 approaches the steady-state eigenvector, as in Strang's California/Massachusetts population model. Fourier series reuse projection onto an orthogonal basis: the coefficients of f in 1, cos x, sin x, ... are inner products in function space.
key_ideas: eigenvalues of A^T equal those of A

units.title: Exam 2 Review
units.part: Unit II: Least Squares, Determinants and Eigenvalues
units.summary: Review of Unit II, the heart of the course: orthogonal matrices and Gram-Schmidt, projections and least squares, determinant properties and cofactors, and eigenvalues and diagonalization, practised on sample questions about projection matrices, least-squares fits and eigenvalues of special matrices.

units.title: Exam 2
units.part: Unit II: Least Squares, Determinants and Eigenvalues
units.summary: The Unit II exam with solutions: determinants of matrices built from orthonormal vectors q1, q2, q3, a least-squares line through 21 equally spaced measurements, projection matrices P_Q and P_A from Gram-Schmidt and the formula for the next vector q4, and determinants of 4 by 4 matrices with one repeated entry along the first row and column.

units.title: Symmetric Matrices and Positive Definiteness
units.part: Unit III: Positive Definite Matrices and Applications
units.summary: Real symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors, so A = Q Lambda Q^T is a sum of projections lambda_k q_k q_k^T. The signs of the pivots match the signs of the eigenvalues, and positive definite matrices are the symmetric ones whose eigenvalues, pivots and upper-left determinants are all positive.
key_ideas: spectral theorem A = Q Lambda Q^T

units.title: Complex Matrices; Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)
units.part: Unit III: Positive Definite Matrices and Applications
units.summary: Complex vectors use the conjugate transpose: |z|^2 = conj(z)^T z, Hermitian matrices generalise symmetric ones and unitary matrices generalise orthogonal ones. The Fourier matrix F_n built from powers of w = e^(2 pi i / n) has orthogonal columns, and the fast Fourier transform splits F_n into two copies of F_(n/2), cutting the work from n^2 to about (n/2) log2 n.

units.title: Positive Definite Matrices and Minima
units.part: Unit III: Positive Definite Matrices and Applications
units.summary: Four equivalent tests for positive definiteness (positive eigenvalues, positive leading determinants, positive pivots, x^T A x > 0 for x != 0) connect to calculus: the matrix of second derivatives decides a minimum, completing the square is elimination, and x^T A x = 1 is an ellipse or ellipsoid whose axes point along the eigenvectors.

units.title: Similar Matrices and Jordan Form
units.part: Unit III: Positive Definite Matrices and Applications
units.summary: A^T A is positive definite when A has independent columns. Similar matrices B = M^-1 A M share eigenvalues and numbers of independent eigenvectors, so each family has a simplest member: the diagonal Lambda when A is diagonalizable, otherwise a Jordan form with one Jordan block per independent eigenvector.
key_ideas: similar matrices B = M^-1 A M

units.title: Singular Value Decomposition
units.part: Unit III: Positive Definite Matrices and Applications
units.summary: Every matrix factors as A = U Sigma V^T: an orthonormal basis v of the row space maps to an orthonormal basis u of the column space with A v_i = sigma_i u_i. The v's are eigenvectors of A^T A, the sigma^2 are its eigenvalues and the u's come from A A^T, worked on A = [[4, 4], [-3, 3]] and on a rank-one example with a nullspace.
key_ideas: eigenvectors of A^T A and A A^T
orthonormal bases for the four subspaces

units.title: Linear Transformations and their Matrices
units.part: Unit III: Positive Definite Matrices and Applications
units.summary: A transformation is linear when T(v + w) = T(v) + T(w) and T(cv) = cT(v); projections and rotations are linear, shifting the plane is not. Once input and output bases are chosen, every linear T is a matrix whose j-th column records T of the j-th basis vector, so even differentiation of polynomials becomes a matrix.
key_ideas: matrix of T in chosen bases

units.title: Change of Basis; Image Compression
units.part: Unit III: Positive Definite Matrices and Applications
units.summary: Image and video compression switch from the standard pixel basis to a better one (Fourier cosines as in JPEG's 8 by 8 blocks, or Haar wavelets) and keep only the large coefficients. Changing basis by W turns the matrix of a transformation into the similar matrix W^-1 A W, which is diagonal in an eigenvector basis.

units.title: Left and Right Inverses; Pseudoinverse
units.part: Unit III: Positive Definite Matrices and Applications
units.summary: Full column rank gives a left inverse (A^T A)^-1 A^T and full row rank a right inverse A^T (A A^T)^-1. For any matrix, A maps the row space one-to-one onto the column space; the pseudoinverse A+ = V Sigma+ U^T inverts that map and gives the shortest least-squares solution.
key_ideas: row space to column space is invertible

units.title: Exam 3 Review
units.part: Unit III: Positive Definite Matrices and Applications
units.summary: Review of Unit III through sample problems on eigenvalues and eigenvectors, du/dt = Au and e^(At), symmetric and positive definite matrices, similar matrices and the SVD; elimination is set aside because it does not preserve eigenvalues.

units.title: Exam 3
units.part: Unit III: Positive Definite Matrices and Applications
units.summary: The Unit III exam with solutions: what it means for every singular value to equal 1 (A is orthogonal), writing B = H Lambda H^-1 and (B + I)^-1 from an orthonormal Hadamard-type eigenvector matrix H, powers of A through diagonalization, and classifying matrices as symmetric, orthogonal, singular or positive (semi)definite.

units.title: Final Course Review
units.part: Final Exam
units.summary: The last review lecture solves past final-exam questions with the whole course: the four subspaces, projections and least squares, eigenvalues, and the special matrices (symmetric, orthogonal, projection, permutation, positive definite), followed by a recitation that works one full final-exam problem.

units.title: Final Exam
units.part: Final Exam
units.summary: A nine-question final with solutions spanning the course: special solutions and rref of a 3 by 4 matrix, the inverse of a triangular U, rank of block matrices, independent columns and A^T A, energy x^T A x in an eigenvector basis, Gram-Schmidt, eigenvalues, projections and least squares, and a tridiagonal 3-2-1 matrix.

units.title: Final 18.06 Lecture (2023)
units.part: Final Exam
units.summary: Strang's farewell 18.06 lecture from May 2023, added to this OCW course: tributes from colleagues around a compact review that runs elimination on a 3 by 3 system, then finds rank 2 and two special solutions for a 3 by 4 matrix whose third row is the sum of the first two, ending on row rank = column rank.
